title: Dharmasvamin in the Ashes
subtitle: A Tibetan Pilgrim Among Fallen Viharas
era: Khalji raids and aftermath, c. 1193-1235 CE
moral: Honest memory faces loss without inventing certainty.

sources.citation: Biography of Dharmasvamin, visit of 1234-35, trans. George Roerich (1959)
sources.note: Primary eyewitness-derived account of Nalanda's reduced survival.
Primary Islamic source for Bakhtiyar Khalji's Bihar campaign and Odantapuri destruction.

sources.citation: Frederick Asher, Nalanda (2015); Johan Elverskog, Buddhism and Islam on the Silk Road (2010)
sources.note: Recent source-critical scholarship on destruction, survival and myth.

panels.shot: wide, low-angle shot of ruined Nalanda towers silhouetted against a hazy sky, with two robed figures tiny in the foreground

dialogue.text: Four decades after Bakhtiyar Khalji’s fiery raids, Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvamin reaches shattered Nalanda and finds, not empty ashes, but an old master and a last, fragile circle of learning.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Dharmasvamin’s determined face as he studies a worn palm-leaf manuscript by a flickering lamp

dialogue.text: In the high monasteries of Tibet, Dharmasvamin hears of Nalanda—the famed Indian university of the old Pala kings, now spoken of in whispers as broken, burned, perhaps gone.

panels.shot: wide shot of caravan moving across a dusty north Indian plain, with Dharmasvamin riding alongside traders

dialogue.text: He sets out for the Ganga lands around 1234, crossing plains now ruled by new sultans, where rumours speak of horse-riding Khalji armies and ruined viharas in Bihar.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of the Mangala Gauri hill at Gaya with scattered shrines and pilgrims, Dharmasvamin a small figure climbing

dialogue.text: At Gaya and Bodhgaya he sees signs of decline—few monks, more lay pilgrims—but still living worship. Nalanda lies further, its fate less certain, its name a test for his faith.

panels.shot: sweeping wide shot of Odantapuri’s hilltop ruins with smoke stains, Dharmasvamin approaching cautiously from below

dialogue.text: In Bihar he hears of Odantapuri, once a great monastery-city. Minhaj-i-Siraj later records how Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked it—its stronghold stormed, its defenders and monks destroyed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Dharmasvamin speaking with wary local villagers at the edge of ruined monastic walls

dialogue.text: Local memories echo the chronicle: mounted troops, sudden assault, flames, monasteries stripped of wealth. Buddhist institutions, once backed by Pala kings, had become exposed targets.

panels.shot: long shot of Dharmasvamin walking alone along a dirt track toward Nalanda’s mounds, the horizon hazy

dialogue.text: Then he turns north-west, following names half-lost in speech, until the great compound of Nalanda rises before him—not as soaring halls, but as scorched brick and fallen towers.

panels.shot: wide ground-level shot moving through charred, collapsed halls of Nalanda with Dharmasvamin stepping carefully

dialogue.text: Archaeologists later see in these layers signs of catastrophic burning. Dharmasvamin sees it with his own eyes: ceilings gone, many houses empty, the great libraries silent and dark.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot inside a small surviving hall where Rahula Śrībhadra sits teaching a handful of students

dialogue.text: But Nalanda is not empty. In one hall, Dharmasvamin finds Rahula Śrībhadra—the old abbot, now frail, still teaching a handful of students amid ruin, keeping Vinaya discipline alive.

panels.shot: close-up on Rahula Śrībhadra’s lined face as he gestures calmly, with Dharmasvamin bowing in respect

dialogue.speaker: Rahula Śrībhadra
dialogue.text: The halls may fall, son, but the precepts do not fall so easily.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modest patron, Jayadeva, speaking with Dharmasvamin and Rahula near a crumbling gateway

dialogue.text: A local lay supporter named Jayadeva helps sustain this remnant. With his patronage, a few cells and halls function, proof that monastic learning clings on through local ties and quiet generosity.

panels.shot: interior medium shot of Dharmasvamin reciting texts before Rahula and the students in a surviving hall

dialogue.text: Dharmasvamin studies there for some months, his biography noting lessons, ordination rituals, and the strange contrast: a once vast university now reduced to a few teachers and scattered pupils.

panels.shot: wide shot of Nalanda ruins at dusk, with distant silhouettes of armed riders suggesting the new power

dialogue.text: Around them, the wider order has shifted. Ghurid and Khalji power presses into Bihar; old land grants lapse; monastic wealth and strategic positions make viharas obvious targets in a contested frontier.

panels.shot: close-up of Dharmasvamin writing on palm leaves by lamplight, with a glimpse of ruined structures outside

dialogue.text: He notes no three-month inferno, no single apocalyptic night, but a landscape of burning, flight, and survival—in which Nalanda is damaged, diminished, yet stubbornly not dead.

panels.shot: medium shot of Dharmasvamin taking leave of Rahula Śrībhadra at a broken gateway, both clasping hands

dialogue.speaker: Dharmasvamin
dialogue.text: I will carry Nalanda’s memory north, just as you carried its rule here.

panels.shot: wide shot of Dharmasvamin’s figure receding along the road, Nalanda’s ruins behind, sky brightening ahead

dialogue.text: His biography, shaped by disciples, later carries this scene into Tibetan memory—a rare, sober eyewitness bridge between the age of Pala-supported universities and their fractured aftermath.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a charred stupa base overgrown with grass, with faint figures of future pilgrims in the far background

dialogue.text: Dharmasvamin and Rahula Śrībhadra show Nalanda not as pure legend or simple end, but as a real place scarred by violence where learning flickered on—reminding us that honest memory holds both loss and survival together.
